paras: The attempted lynching of Harry Irvin took place at Monteith, Georgia, on 9 August 1903, when an armed mob pursued Irvin, a Black man accused of criminally assaulting an 11-year-old girl in Effingham County, and surrounded the house where he had taken refuge. Constable J. A. Northcutt persuaded the mob to let him take Irvin to Savannah, and the two left on a train that night. The Savannah Morning News reported the episode as a narrowly averted clash, noting that a crowd of Irvin's own relatives and friends later arrived to demand his release.

According to the Savannah Morning News, the alleged assault took place in Effingham County on the afternoon of 9 August. A mob of "fifty or sixty armed men," led by brothers of the girl, then pursued Irvin "through the country" and ran him into a house at Monteith. The mob was denied entrance to the house, and the men were preparing to enter by force when Constable Northcutt arrived.

The constable prevailed on the men to consent to Irvin's removal to Savannah, though the paper said some in the crowd "wished to deal with the negro summarily" and caused trouble. The crowd stayed after nightfall, and later that night a second crowd made up of Irvin's brothers and friends arrived and demanded his release. Serious trouble between the two parties was, in the paper's words, "for some time imminent"; the surviving text breaks off at this point. Northcutt boarded an incoming train "hurriedly" with Irvin and reached Savannah that night.
No report of an arrest of mob members, a hearing or a trial of Irvin was found in the coverage.

The only report found ran on page 8 of the Savannah Morning News on 10 August 1903 under the headlines "Pursued by a Mob" and "Armed Men Determined, but Officer Hustled His Man on Train to Savannah." The story centered on the constable's "thrilling experience" and "quick work," and it described the girl as "wronged" and Irvin as "the offender," treating the accusation as settled. It named Irvin's race but not the mob's, and it did not condemn the mob. No coverage in other white papers or in the Black press was found.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News local report (constable's return)
accounts.gist: An armed mob led by the girl's brothers chased Irvin into a house at Monteith and was about to force entry when Constable Northcutt arrived, talked the men into letting him take Irvin to Savannah, and left hurriedly by train; a crowd of Irvin's relatives and friends later confronted the mob.

framing.detail: Headlines stress danger and the officer's rescue ('ARMED MEN DETERMINED', 'Constable's Quick Work') while the text calls the girl 'wronged' and Irvin 'the offender', treating the accusation as fact without endorsing the mob.
